name: Algebraization, Inclusion-Exclusion and Convolution Methods for Subset Sum
description: A line of algebraic techniques that evaluate a Subset Sum (or Knapsack) dynamic program without storing its pseudo-polynomial table. Lokshtanov and Nederlof (STOC 2010) formalize the DP as an arithmetic circuit over a ring of tables, where the expensive operation is convolution, then apply a linear transform (Discrete Fourier Transform for integer-indexed tables, zeta/Mobius transform - i.e. inclusion-exclusion over the subset lattice - for subset-indexed tables) so that convolution becomes pointwise multiplication; a single desired coefficient can then be computed in pseudo-polynomial time and polynomial space. This yields the first pseudo-polynomial-time, polynomial-space algorithms for Subset Sum and Knapsack, and via inclusion-exclusion the same idea gives polynomial-space algorithms for Weighted Set Cover, Weighted Steiner Tree and TSP. A parallel exponential-time line uses generating functions and inclusion-exclusion to attack worst-case instances in exponential time with polynomial space, culminating in the Bansal-Garg-Nederlof-Vyas O*(2^{0.86n})-time polynomial-space Monte Carlo algorithm.
worst_case_time: Two separate regimes. (1) Pseudo-polynomial: O~(n^3 t log t) time for Subset Sum and O~(n^4 log^2(vw) * v w) time for Knapsack (Lokshtanov-Nederlof, STOC 2010). (2) Exponential-time, polynomial-space: O*(2^{0.86n}) time for Subset Sum and Knapsack, assuming random read-only access to exponentially many random bits (Bansal-Garg-Nederlof-Vyas, FOCS 2017); randomized k-Sum variants use O(n^{k-0.5} polylog n) time. The best worst-case exponential time independently of space remains O*(2^{0.5n}) (Horowitz-Sahni 1974; Schroeppel-Shamir 1979), shaved only by polynomial factors in 2023 (Chen-Jin-Randolph-Servedio, 2^{n/2}/poly(n)).
space_complexity: Pseudo-polynomial regime: O~(n^2) space for Subset Sum and O~(n^2 log(vw)) for Knapsack (Lokshtanov-Nederlof, STOC 2010), replacing Bellman's O(t) / O(w) table space. Exponential regime: polynomial space, poly(n, log t) (Bansal-Garg-Nederlof-Vyas 2017); the low-space variant of Jin-Vyas (SODA 2021) uses O(log(nt)) space; Kane (2010) gave an earlier deterministic log-space algorithm. The inclusion-exclusion line for Steiner Tree uses O*(c) space (Nederlof, Algorithmica 2013).
model: Word RAM / unit-cost arithmetic RAM. The algebraization framework is formalized as a circuit over the ring of tables R[S] with pointwise addition and convolution, evaluated through the DFT (integer-indexed tables) or the zeta/Mobius transform (subset-indexed tables), either exactly over C or over Z_p. Bansal-Garg-Nederlof-Vyas assume random read-only access to exponentially many random bits (a mild random-oracle-like assumption). [uncertain] exact bit-model details of the DFT-based evaluation in Lokshtanov-Nederlof.
randomized_or_deterministic: Mixed. Lokshtanov-Nederlof's algebraization and Nederlof's inclusion-exclusion algorithms are deterministic; Bansal-Garg-Nederlof-Vyas is Monte Carlo (high success probability, error probability inverse polynomial, under the random-bits assumption); Jin-Vyas is randomized; Kane's log-space algorithm is deterministic. [uncertain] the precise error probability and whether Bansal-Garg-Nederlof-Vyas is one-sided.
time_space_tradeoff_curve: The algebraization framework exposes a tradeoff parameterized by the table dimension d and the ring/table size N: computing one output coefficient costs time O~(|C| * N * polylog N) and space O((|C| + log N) * polylog N), where |C| is the circuit size; space is essentially the circuit size, not the table size. Jin-Vyas give an explicit Subset Sum time-space tradeoff (e.g. O~(n t) time at O(log(nt)) space; O~(n^{1+eps} t) time for any eps>0). Otherwise each result is a single point: pseudo-polynomial O~(n^3 t) time / O~(n^2) space; exponential O*(2^{0.86n}) time / poly space; O*(2^{0.5n}) time / O*(2^{0.25n}) space (Schroeppel-Shamir).
numerical_exponent_and_record_year: Exponential regime: time exponent 0.86n with polynomial space, Bansal-Garg-Nederlof-Vyas, FOCS 2017 (SICOMP 2018). Pseudo-polynomial regime: O~(n^3 t log t) time with O~(n^2) space, Lokshtanov-Nederlof, STOC 2010. Best unconditional worst-case exponential time still 0.5n (1979/2023).
problem_variant: Vanilla Subset Sum (decision) and Knapsack in the pseudo-polynomial regime; the algebraization/inclusion-exclusion framework also covers Weighted Set Cover, Weighted Steiner Tree, Traveling Salesman, Binary Linear Programming with few constraints, and k-Sum. The Bansal-Garg-Nederlof-Vyas result handles Subset Sum, Knapsack and Binary Linear Programming; its O(n^{k-0.5}) bound is for random k-Sum.
applies_to: General (all) n-integer Subset Sum instances in the pseudo-polynomial-time / polynomial-space setting (Lokshtanov-Nederlof, Nederlof) and worst-case instances in the exponential-time / polynomial-space setting (Bansal-Garg-Nederlof-Vyas, Jin-Vyas). The generating-function coefficient-extraction technique in Jin-Vyas constructs a polynomial with a zero x^t coefficient for NO-instances and a nonzero x^t coefficient for YES-instances with high probability.
coefficient_set: C = {0,1} for Subset Sum (each item chosen or not). Knapsack uses the same binary selection with different weight/value coefficients. The subset-indexed version works over the Boolean lattice (zeta/Mobius / inclusion-exclusion), and the integer-indexed version over products of cyclic groups (DFT).
density_regime: Two faces. The pseudo-polynomial algorithms are efficient when the target t (or capacity w) is small, i.e. the low-density / small-item regime (polynomial in log t only). The Bansal-Garg-Nederlof-Vyas algorithm targets general worst-case instances and uses anti-concentration of subset sums, which is most useful in dense regimes; it is not density-restricted. The generating-function/Jin-Vyas approach also targets small t (pseudo-polynomial in t) with logarithmic space.
solution_regime: General decision problem (no promise of many solutions) for both the pseudo-polynomial and the exponential polynomial-space algorithms.
cardinality_constraint: No fixed-cardinality (Hamming-layer) constraint is assumed. Internally the subset-indexed transform (zeta/Mobius) works over the subset lattice and can encode cardinality when needed, but the target problems are unconstrained Subset Sum / Knapsack.
key_technique: Algebraization of dynamic programming: express the DP recurrence as an arithmetic circuit over the ring of tables R[S] (pointwise addition, convolution), then apply a linear transform that diagonalizes convolution - the Discrete Fourier Transform for tables indexed by Z_{N1} x ... x Z_{Nd}, and the zeta/Mobius (inclusion-exclusion) transform for tables indexed by subsets. Because the transformed circuit uses only pointwise operations and singleton constants, one output entry f[g] is recovered by the inverse transform sum f[g] = (1/N) * sum_j e^{-(g . t) . j} (F(f))[j], where each term (F(f))[j] is computed by a small O~(log N)-size circuit without materializing any table. Inclusion-exclusion / Mobius inversion and generating-function coefficient extraction are the subset-lattice and polynomial-product special cases.
core_idea: Convolution (adding two DP tables of subset sums) is the memory-hungry step, but it becomes pointwise multiplication after a Fourier/Mobius transform. Pointwise products need no intermediate tables, so the DP can be evaluated 'entry by entry' with space proportional to the circuit depth/size rather than to the table. In particular the generating function prod_i (1 + x^{a_i}) has x^t coefficient equal to the number of subsets summing to t, and extracting that single coefficient via the transform avoids storing the degree-t polynomial. The same diagonalization is why inclusion-exclusion turns subset-lattice convolutions into pointwise products. In the exponential setting, anti-concentration and implicit (cycle-finding) search over an exponentially large but implicitly represented space replace the table.
reduction_pipeline: Subset Sum / Knapsack DP -> arithmetic circuit over (R[S], circle-plus, convolution) with singleton constants -> DFT (integer-indexed) or zeta/Mobius inversion (subset-indexed) -> pointwise evaluation -> inverse transform to read one coefficient. Generating-function view: prod_{i} (1 + x^{a_i}) mod x^{t+1}, coefficient extraction by roots of unity / DFT. Exponential line: Subset Sum -> implicit large-list intersection / cycle finding -> O*(2^{0.86n}) poly-space. Inclusion-exclusion line: set covering / Steiner Tree -> subset-lattice zeta transform -> polynomial space.
constructive_vs_existential: Constructive: the algorithms compute the relevant coefficient / decide the instance, and standard self-reduction recovers an explicit witness. Bansal-Garg-Nederlof-Vyas is constructive (returns a witness list).
search_vs_decision_witness: Decides feasibility and, via self-reduction, returns an explicit witness; constructivity is established in the works (the coefficient is nonzero exactly when a solution exists, and Bansal-Garg-Nederlof-Vyas output an actual subset).
obstacle_to_2n3: The pseudo-polynomial algebraization algorithms run in time polynomial in t, which is exponential in n for large targets; they cannot give a 2^{c n} bound at all. The exponential polynomial-space line is much slower than the O*(2^{0.5n}) MITM barrier: Bansal-Garg-Nederlof-Vyas run in O*(2^{0.86n}) and Jin-Vyas in O~(n t) / O~(n^{1+eps} t), all well above 2^{n/2}, let alone 2^{n/3}. Algebraization saves space, not time: it diagonalizes the same exhaustive DP, so no parameter choice reduces the exponent below 0.5n. Reaching 2^{n/3} would require a genuine time breakthrough that the transform machinery does not provide.
barrier_evidence: The algebraic method is a space-saving transformation of the same exhaustive DP, so it cannot beat the O*(2^{0.5n}) worst-case time barrier. Abboud, Bringmann, Hermelin and Shabtay (SODA 2019) give SETH-based lower bounds and time-space tradeoffs for Subset Sum (when time equals space, a t^{1-eps} 2^{o(n)} bound would refute SETH). The Bansal-Garg-Nederlof-Vyas result also depends on the random-read-only-bits assumption, and later work removed it using a pseudorandom hash family, indicating the assumption is mild but not vacuous.
open_questions: Can the polynomial-space exponential algorithms (Bansal-Garg-Nederlof-Vyas, Jin-Vyas) be derandomized / made independent of the random-bits assumption, or fully deterministic? Can the 0.86n exponent be pushed below 0.5n while retaining polynomial space? Is there a tight SETH-based lower bound for the time-space tradeoff of the exact decision problem matching the algebraic upper bounds? Can algebraization be combined with the representation technique / Howgrave-Graham-Joux filtering to gain both time and space?
conditional_hypothesis: SETH underlies the conditional time-space lower bounds (Abboud-Bringmann-Hermelin-Shabtay). The upper bounds themselves are unconditional, except that Bansal-Garg-Nederlof-Vyas assume random read-only access to exponentially many random bits. No lattice or k-SUM hardness assumption is needed for the algebraic algorithms.
worst_case_vs_average_case_guarantee: Lokshtanov-Nederlof and Nederlof are worst-case deterministic (all instances). Bansal-Garg-Nederlof-Vyas are Monte Carlo with high success probability on all instances (under the random-bits assumption); their k-Sum corollary is for random instances. Jin-Vyas is randomized with small error probability. So the line is predominantly worst-case (randomized) except for the explicit random-k-Sum statement.
cryptographic_regime: Relevant to knapsack/subset-sum cryptanalysis: the pseudo-polynomial polynomial-space algorithm is efficient exactly in the low-target (small-density) regime where lattice and meet-in-the-middle attacks are classically applied, and the algebraic transforms are the same DFT/inclusion-exclusion tools used in representation-technique attacks. Bansal-Garg-Nederlof-Vyas's anti-concentration perspective is used to argue about density-1 and dense knapsack instances. These are asymptotic complexity results and not concrete attacks.
pseudopolynomial_interaction: This is the central interaction: the algebraization framework is precisely a pseudo-polynomial-time, polynomial-space replacement for Bellman's pseudo-polynomial-space DP, and the generating-function/coefficient-extraction method is pseudopolynomial in t. It combines naturally with DP over subset-sum values and with inclusion-exclusion counting, and it is the space analogue of the ordinary O(nt) DP.

empirical_evidence: None found. The results are asymptotic running-time and space bounds; the papers report no benchmarks. The only quantitative artifacts are numeric parameter optimizations (table dimensions, moduli) that determine the stated exponents.
implementation_artifact: none found (no released reference implementation of the algebraization or Bansal-Garg-Nederlof-Vyas algorithms was located).
verification_method: Re-derive the DFT and zeta/Mobius diagonalization (convolution -> pointwise product), then check Theorem 4.3 in Lokshtanov-Nederlof: the transformed circuit C' over (C, +, .) has the same graph as C and evaluates F(f) pointwise; verify the inverse-transform formula f[g] = (1/N) sum_j e^{-(g.t).j} (F(f))[j] and that computing each (F(f))[j] uses only O~(log N) size. For the generating-function view, check that prod_i (1 + x^{a_i}) has x^t coefficient equal to the number of solutions and that coefficient extraction can be done in polynomial space. For the exponential line, reproduce the list-intersection/cycle-finding analysis in arXiv:1612.02788.
